entry.title: On the Life of An Astronomer Hermit and Astrology
entry.content:
In this post, we hypothesize how astrology might have come into existence as a natural consequence of a hermit living alone for a long time in Nature with the aim of coming up with a theory as to why prominent events occur at specific times. This hermit would be similar to that in Thanu Padmanabhan's Akbar story. Note that we make absolutely no claims about the efficacy of astrology whatsoever.

Imagine a hermit, H, living in a hut and interacting only with Nature. In addition, imagine H to have a good knowledge of astronomy. H's aim is to try to come up with a theory as to why prominent events happened in their past at specific times. When H's mind analyzes the events happening around them and those that have happened to them and to others in the past, the only movement they know is that in the Nature around them and that of the planets via their knowledge of astronomy, that's the only sense of Time they have.

It's in the nature of the mind to start correlating planetary motion with the events that have happened in their own lives and those in the lives of others, because H is not aware of any other movement other than the planetary movement known via the mathematics of astronomy and the movement in the Nature around them. This may be how astrology came into existence.

Thus, we hypothesize that it's in the nature of the mind of a knowledgeable hermit to correlate planetary motion known via mathematics with prominent events, if their aim is to come up with a theory to explain why prominent events occur at specific times.

entry.title: On Sound in Nyaya Sutra
entry.content:
In this post, we clarify our understanding of what sound is in texts like Nyaya Sutra. Previously, we hypothesized that Shruti is heard via ether[1]. We have also written about how the perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias[2]. We use these two ideas to hypothesize our understanding of sound (shabdah).

We first give the traditional scientific understanding of sound and contrast it with what we believe is the understanding in texts like Nyaya Sutra.

The scientific understanding[3] is to characterize sound as a pressure wave, with frequency being the parameter that determines whether the wave can be heard by the human ear or not. The ear converts the pressure wave to an auditory signal that is sent to the brain.

Now, we contrast this with what we believe is sound as characterized by Nyaya Sutra. As we have written about how perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias[2], we believe that when everything is to be understood with only the mind, we would need to define the ear in an abstract manner, that is, as a concept. So, the concept of the ear is that it provides input to the mind. Now, with this understanding, all auditory input that the mind can understand is from the ear, irrespective of whether it can be heard by others or not. So, sound is not a pressure wave with this understanding; it is what the mind can interpret as coming from the concept of the ears. The physical ears that we have become the physical manifestation of the concept of the ears. And sound becomes what the mind can interpret as auditory input, and it may or may not be a pressure wave or be heard by others.

Thus, we have explained what we believe is sound as characterized by texts like Nyaya Sutra.

[2] https://m-chaturvedi.github.io/blog/040/

[3] https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/how-do-we-hear

entry.title: On Ether
entry.content:
In this post, we hypothesize about how Shruti is heard [1]. We first define sound. We define sound as what is heard by the human ear and interpreted by the mind. That is, we don't define it as a pressure wave requiring a physical medium, but define it from the point of view of the human ear.

We argue that sound has two manifestations, the physical and the abstract, and two mediums of travel, the physical and the ether. Characterization of sound as a pressure wave is the common scientific understanding. In this post, we argue that sound could also have an ethereal character if defined from the point of view of the human ear.

First, we note something about the ears. We observe that it is scientifically known that the sense of sound is active even in deep sleep [2]. In a previous post, we proposed an experiment to characterize perceived reality as a cognitive bias [3]; we refer to this state of mind as S. We hypothesize that the mind in S is similar to deep sleep as far as the sense of hearing is concerned, and that the sense of hearing is still intact in S, although the physical manifestation of sound is absent, i.e., we are in a silent place.

We hypothesize that we hear sound when we are in a state of deep concentration, and the mind remembers it when we come out of the state. This can be easily seen in day-to-day life. When someone is deeply concentrating on something like a computer program or a book, and someone says something to them, they hear it but don't react to it immediately, and react to it after they are out of the state of deep concentration, a few seconds or a fraction of a second later.

This is what happens when our mind is meditating in deep concentration: the sense of hearing is intact, and we remember what we were hearing via ether when we come out of the concentration. We believe that this is how Shruti is heard, via ether. We also note that in texts like the Nyaya Sutra, the sense of hearing is connected to ether, not air [4].

Thus, in this post, we argued how Shruti is heard from ether.

entry.title: On the Importance of Individual Responsibility in the Bhagavad Gita
entry.content:
In this post, we highlight a few aspects of the Bhagavad Gita and hypothesize why they are so. We note that our observations are based on intuition rather than study.

We observe that:

  1. Although the story of the Gita is recalled by Sanjaya as part of the Mahabharata, which is a Smriti, the Bhagavad Gita is told to an individual, Arjuna, who is professionally a warrior. It is not told to a group of people.
  2. It's told by Krishna, who is the charioteer.
  3. It's told on a battlefield, where there are a lot of people, but it is said in such a divine way that only Arjuna can hear it.

We believe that it is told in such a way because Arjuna, who is a warrior whose duty it is to fight for dharma, is in doubt about whether to fight or not, because his friends and family are his opponents. This knowledge of why he must fight in order to restore Nature's equilibrium, i.e., dharma, is realized at the individual level and not in groups. We believe that this happens by reflecting and meditating on what is happening around us, both of which are individual-focused activities.

Krishna acts as a charioteer, and not as a co-fighter, telling us that Nature guides the individual by taking them to the right places when they act on the path of dharma.

Even when in groups, divine knowledge is given at the individual level, as we wrote about before, that the source of knowledge is within, not outside.

Thus, we made a few observations and argued that the Bhagavad Gita emphasizes individual responsibility.

entry.title: On Language and Propaganda
entry.content:
In this post, we explain a way in which propaganda is spread. We first propose an observation about when a person P says a statement X in a context C:

In a context C, P said a statement X if and only if P can say not(X), i.e., the opposite of X. If not(X) cannot be said in context C, then there exists some underlying propaganda being spread while saying X.

We now give examples of our observation for different contexts:

Politics: Consider two political parties, A and B. A spokesperson for party A says that party B is corrupt. Here, the context is political, and the complementary statement would be that party A's spokesperson says party B is honest. But we know that party A would never explicitly praise party B. Thus, the complementary statement cannot be said. So, party A's spokesperson's propaganda is to promote party A over B, no matter what.

Dating: Consider a man A trying to woo a woman B. A says to B that she is very beautiful. Here, the context is dating. The complementary statement would be A saying that B is not beautiful. But we know that A would not say that if they want to have a chance of dating B. Thus, the complementary statement cannot be said. So, A's propaganda is to make B feel good, not tell them the truth.

Selling a product: Consider a CEO announcing a product, A, and consider a competing product, B. The CEO says that A is better than B overall. Here, the context is marketing. The complementary statement would be that B is better than A. But we know that the CEO would never make such a statement because the laws of capitalism prevent it. So, the propaganda that the CEO is spreading is that his company's product A is better than others, whether it is objectively so or not.

Day-to-day Life: Consider A wishing B a happy birthday. The complement of this would be A wishing B a sad birthday. But we know that this would not happen in a general context. Here, the propaganda being spread is that birthdays are inherently good.

War: Consider country A's spokesperson saying to country B that country A is going to attack country B tonight. Now the complementary statement would be A's spokesperson saying that they are not going to attack B tonight. But we know that this rarely happens. So, here the propaganda is that conveying that an attack is going to happen is more important than conveying that an attack is not going to happen.

So, we gave a few examples of how not being able to say the complement of a statement in a context inherently means that some underlying propaganda is being spread.

entry.title: On an Aspect of Buddhism
entry.content:
In this post, we discuss an aspect of Buddhism. Specifically, we put forth our opinion on why being a universal ruler, Chakravartin, is equivalent to being the Buddha, the enlightened one.

At the birth of Siddhartha Gautama, the sages had predicted that he'd be a universal ruler or become enlightened[1]. We believe that this is so because the two are equivalent states theoretically.

In theory, being in control of everything is the same as being detached from everything. In practice, this manifests as acting in a detached way, i.e., acting with the body and senses while having the right abstract representation of the perceived reality in the mind, which, we believe, is essentially Karma yoga.

As we've discussed in a previous post, perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias if it is to be understood with only the mind. The Buddha, we believe, is the perfect scientist who's perceiving reality as a cognitive bias and is meditating on the abstract representation of the perceived reality, i.e., the Buddha is understanding the perceived reality instead of experiencing it. The Chakravartin, the universal ruler, is in control of the whole universe because he has the right abstract representation of the universe in his mind; in other words, he interacts with the perceived reality with his body and senses while having the right abstract representation of it in his mind. Just like in engineering, once the underlying scientific laws are understood, one can engineer perfect machines and structures. The universal ruler, having understood and internalized all the universal laws, becomes a great king.

Thus, we see that one could argue that being a universal ruler requires acting with sensory detachment from the perceived reality, and so does being in the enlightened state, the only difference being that one doesn't act at all in the Buddha-like state, making the two states theoretically equivalent.

We end this post with an interesting Hindi/Urdu saying by the 14th century Sufi saint Kabir who influenced Bhakti yoga:

Phikr gayi, chinta miti, man hua beparwaah
Jinko kachu na chahiye, wo shaahon ke shaah

Translation by ChatGPT:

Worry is gone, anxiety has vanished, and the mind has become carefree.
Those who desire nothing are the kings of kings.

[1] From wiki: According to later biographical legends, during the birth celebrations, the hermit seer Asita journeyed from his mountain abode, analysed the child for the "32 marks of a great man" and then announced that he would either become a great king (chakravartin) or a great religious leader.

entry.title: On Vulnerability
entry.content:
In this post, we argue why vulnerability is an important component in personal relationships.

We first define personal relationships with others. We define personal relationships with others as the outward projection of the relationship we have with ourselves. In other words, personal relationships are governed by internal laws [1]. Note that we don't differentiate between close and distant personal relationships, like those with a close friend or an audience; we just define them as relationships that affect one personally.

The more true and authentic we are with ourselves, the more vulnerable we are with ourselves. And the more vulnerable we are with ourselves, the more authentically we can connect with others. The authenticity can come from two sources: emotions and reason [2]. That is, interpreting ourselves to be the physical body or not, i.e., characterizing the perceived reality as a cognitive bias or not [3].

We can study this in two professions that are at the two ends of the spectrum: the philosopher and the artist. The philosopher, who interprets themselves to be the mind, connecting with others using reason, and the artist, who interprets themselves to be the body, connecting with others using emotions.

Both philosophers and artists can connect with a large audience at a personal level. The philosopher is very honest with others, i.e., they share their mind in the form of thoughts, which makes them very vulnerable to others, since everyone knows where they stand on many issues, so they can connect with a large audience at a personal level.

The artist is very vulnerable to others because they share their real emotions[4] in the form of the art they create, and thus are capable of connecting to a large audience at a personal level.

Thus we see that both the artist and the philosopher are able to connect with a large audience by being vulnerable, which in turn is a resultant of being authentic with themselves.

entry.title: On the Two Types of Laws and the Two Interpretations of Reality
entry.content:
In this post, we put forth our understanding of how the two interpretations of reality can lead to two types of laws.

We have discussed in a previous post, how perceived reality can be interpreted as a cognitive bias. In this post, we propose that the two interpretations lead to two separate types of laws: internal and external law.

If perceived reality is not interpreted as a cognitive bias, the individual would be represented by their physical manifestation, i.e., by the body. This leads to external law because, with this interpretation, we would need an external (to the body) entity to make and enforce the laws. This is the common type of law we see around us, with police, courts, and books of law.

The second type of law is internal law. This is the law when the whole world is perceived only with the mind, without any inputs from the senses. This typically manifests as the individual not being comfortable with themselves because they have either caused injustice or have been unjustly treated, according to the internal law. Since this interpretation of reality leads to Nirvana as the goal of human existence, internal law typically manifests as ideas like karma, doing penances, etc.

entry.title: The Bhagavad Gita and the Importance of Emotions
entry.content:
In this post, we discuss our interpretation of an aspect of the Geeta. Specifically, how it emphasizes the importance of emotions.

The Geeta is often translated as "The Song of God" [1]. "Geet" means song in various South Asian languages. As we discussed in a previous post on cognitive biases, when the mind is free from sensory perception and thoughts, it senses absolute reality, and it is the emotions that the senses and thoughts create that make up perceived reality [2]. Specifically, there are no emotions involved when the mind senses the absolute reality.

The Geeta, instead of being philosophical text like the Upanishads, is supposed to be remembered as a song [3]. It is important here to emphasize the context in which the Geeta is set. The Geeta takes place on a battlefield where millions of soldiers died [4]. In spite of such a grave context, it is a song.

We note a few properties of songs:

  1. They have a structural pattern in the concrete, i.e., words; they have a rhythm[5]. Or rhyme, in English/Hindi/Urdu poetry.

  2. They have a structural pattern in the abstract, i.e., there is a raga in which they can be sung, or a type of rhythm that they follow.

  3. They are meaningful. They speak to the poet's ability to create meaning while keeping the aforementioned refrains.

  4. They emphasize the importance of emotions in the listeners. That is, listeners can become attached to the song in the concrete—the words of the song—not just the patterns, as in a theorem or a philosophical text, or to a raga.

We believe that the Geeta is a song because it is telling us a truth while also making us attached to the text so that we can remember it more easily. In other words, it leverages and emphasizes the importance of human emotions. We would like to end this post with a quote from Manu Smriti [6]:

सत्यं ब्रूयात प्रियं ब्रूयान्न ब्रूयात सत्यमप्रियम ।
प्रियं च नानृतं ब्रूयादेष धर्मः सनातनः ॥१३८॥

Translation: One should speak the truth. One should speak what is pleasant. One should not speak unpleasant truth. And one should not speak falsehood, even if pleasant. This is the eternal natural law (dharma).

entry.title: Raag Darbari and the Collective Indian Subconscious
entry.content:
In this post we discuss how the famous novel by Shrilal Shukla, Raag Darbari[1][2], correctly pointed out an aspect of the collective Indian subconscious regarding emigration. This was also pointed out to us, in their own way, by a very perceptive American businessman.

Raag Darbari is a subversive novel from 1968. It lays bare the soul of post-independence India, and we believe many of its observations are true even now. The only English-language novel that we’ve come across that comes close to its biting satire is Catch-22.

The author[3] was around 22 years old when India got its independence and later served in the Indian Civil Services, so he had a good idea of how the Indian psyche interacts with artifacts of the British system. The book is written from the perspective of a university-educated protagonist, Ranganath, who comes to his village for vacation and becomes increasingly frustrated by what’s going on there, and in the end decides to leave.

We have read the book more than once, the first time in 2005, and have realized over time that many of the thought patterns in the Indian psyche remain the same now as they were before. We would like to document a couple of excerpts that the frustrated protagonist notes at the end of the book regarding emigration. Much of this remains true even now, as far as the actions of Indians are concerned, but it is covered up with different facades such as higher education, etc. We first note the excerpts in the original Hindi, and then present the English translation by Gillian Wright. We would translate the title of the excerpt as “The Song of Emigration” and would observe that the translation doesn’t quite capture the causticness of the original Hindi.
